"Enormity" refers to the quality of being shockingly, outrageously evil or morally monstrous. It describes not just something big, but something so deeply wrong or horrifying that it goes far beyond normal human behaviour or moral limits.

Think of it as a word that carries weight — specifically, moral weight. When someone uses "enormity," they are saying: this is not just large or significant, this is deeply, shockingly wrong.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine a sliding scale of wrongdoing:

  • Forgetting to call a friend back → minor mistake
  • Cheating on a test → a clear wrong
  • Committing mass murder → horrifying evil

"Enormity" lives at the extreme end of that scale. It is the word you reach for when ordinary words like "badness" or "wrongness" feel too weak to describe what happened.

"The judge spoke of the enormity of the crime."
This means the crime was so shockingly evil that even the judge felt the need to name how monstrous it was.

"He could not sleep, overwhelmed by the enormity of what he had done."
He had done something so deeply wrong that the full moral horror of it was crushing him.

"The world struggled to come to terms with the enormity of the Holocaust."
The Holocaust was not just large in scale — it was a moral catastrophe so extreme that the human mind finds it almost impossible to fully absorb.

Notice how in every case, the word is not just saying "this was a really big thing." It is saying "this was a terrible, outrageous, morally overwhelming thing."
The One Thing Most People Get Wrong

This is very important, and it is a mistake even educated native speakers make.

Many people use "enormity" when they simply mean large size — as in:

"The enormity of the ocean took my breath away."
"She was struck by the enormity of the building."

This is incorrect in careful, formal English. The ocean is not morally wrong. The building is not evil. So "enormity" is the wrong word there.

The correct words for sheer size or scale are:

  • Enormousness ("the enormousness of the ocean")
  • Immensity ("the immensity of the task")
  • Vastness ("the vastness of space")

"Enormity" ≠ enormous size.
"Enormity" = enormous wrongness.

That said, many modern dictionaries now accept the "large size" meaning because it has become so widespread in everyday speech. But in formal writing, academic work, or professional contexts, using "enormity" to mean mere size will look like an error to careful readers. Stick to the traditional meaning and you will never go wrong.

Here is a simple mental test. Before using "enormity," ask yourself:

"Am I talking about something morally monstrous or shockingly evil?"

  • If YES → "enormity" is the right word.
  • If NO → choose "immensity," "vastness," or "enormousness" instead.

Another memory trick: think of "enormity" as containing the idea of an enormously evil norm-breaking — something that violates the norms of human decency on a shocking scale.

Good writers choose "enormity" deliberately because it does something that synonyms like "magnitude" or "scale" simply cannot do — it makes the reader feel the moral horror, not just understand the size. It signals to the reader: stop and sit with how deeply wrong this is.

This is why you will most often encounter "enormity" in writing about:

  • War crimes and atrocities
  • Historical tragedies (genocides, disasters caused by human failure)
  • Serious moral betrayals
  • Moments when a character in a story finally confronts the full weight of what they have done
"Enormity" means the extreme, shocking, and morally overwhelming quality of something deeply evil or wrong — not simply something large.
